::: {.notes}
Status report, not a results talk — the detection / amplitude work is blinded and
in progress, so I'm reporting where the Euclid × CMB-lensing cross-correlation
programme stands rather than headlining a number.

Quick notation, since this audience knows CMB lensing cold but is less familiar
with Euclid's side: δ is Euclid's galaxy density, γ is cosmic shear, and κ is the
SPT-3G D1 lensing map — I'll use these symbols throughout, so it's worth having
them up front.

The frame is this MoU [point to the matrix]: the six two-point spectra of galaxy
density δ, shear γ, and CMB lensing κ — the whole 6×2pt. The cross-hatched cells are
the standard Euclid 3×2pt: clustering, shear, and galaxy–galaxy lensing — what Euclid
does on its own, δ×γ included. What we propose is the shaded cells — and this is a
CMB-only 3×2pt, Louis's framing: of the six spectra, the three that actually involve
CMB-κ are δ×κ, γ×κ, and κκ itself, all three shaded as part of this project.

δ×κ and γ×κ are the genuinely new cross-correlation measurement, the two that bring
in SPT directly. κκ is shaded too — it's part of the CMB-only 3×2pt we're proposing
— but its border is dashed, marking that it comes in differently: it's SPT's own
lensing auto-spectrum, so it's not something we cross-correlate, it folds in at the
likelihood level when we do the joint fit. [say out loud] Galaxy–galaxy lensing,
δ×γ, is cross-hatched only, not shaded — it's a standard Euclid 3×2pt product from
the main 3×2pt group already, not something new we're adding, so later slides that
used to feature it (the data-vector slide) don't anymore.

Why bother: the DES×SPT×Planck 6×2pt (Abbott et al. 2023) tightened Ω_m by ~30% and
S₈ by ~50% over the shear-and-clustering-only 3×2pt, and self-calibrated shear
multiplicative bias at the 5–10% level. We expect the same kind of return for
Euclid — Gatti's forecast has SPT-3G × DR1-South κγ improving the (Ω_m, σ8) figure
of merit ~14% over γγ alone.

This is one piece of a broader CMBX effort: fold our crosses together with the Euclid
3×2pt and it becomes the full 5×2pt, and with κκ in the likelihood, the 6×2pt. [say
out loud]

The MoU is jointly run — I'm the SPT contact, Margherita Lembo the Euclid contact,
with Louis Legrand and the rest of the 3×2pt+κ team.

On timing, and this matters for how we plan the paper relative to Euclid: the Euclid
cosmology products are now scheduled for June 2027 — the public release set at the
May consortium meeting, with DR1 products frozen March 2027. That's later than some
may have assumed (people had ~October in mind), and it sets the pace we're working
at. The upshot the SPT side cares about: we don't have to wait for June 2027 to
publish — a paper can move on its own schedule as long as what we publish matches
what's frozen in the SAS.
:::

## Getting blinding out of the way

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="46%"}
- **Parameter-shift blind**<br>([Muir et al. 2019](https://arxiv.org/abs/1911.05929))
    - same approach as Euclid 3×2pt
- **Cosmology shift** $\Delta\theta \sim \mathcal{U}$:
    - $|\Delta\Omega_m| < 0.1$
    - $|\Delta S_8| < 0.075$
- **Hidden cosmology** $\theta_{\rm blind}$

::: {style="font-size:0.9em; margin-top:-0.6em"}
$$\hat{C}_b^{\rm blind} = \hat{C}_b^{\rm data} + \mathbf{B}_{b\ell}\big[\,C_\ell(\theta_{\rm blind}) - C_\ell(\theta_{\rm fid})\,\big]$$
:::

**All data vectors here are blinded.**

… but low-$z$ bins are not very sensitive.
:::
::: {.column width="54%"}
![](images/spt26_blinding_cosmologies.png){width="98%"}
:::
:::

::: {.notes}
A quick word on blinding, since it sets what every later slide can and can't show.

We use a standard parameter-shift blind — the Muir et al. 2019 scheme, the same family the
Euclid 3×2pt blind uses. (Not the SPT-3G D1 lensing blind, which was procedural rather than a
data-vector cosmology shift.) The recipe is the equation on the
left: pick a hidden cosmology θ_blind, compute the cross-spectra it predicts, take the
difference from the fiducial prediction, window it through the same bandpower operator the data
went through, and add that ΔCℓ to the data vector — and only the data. The theory curves stay
fiducial and the covariance is untouched, so every bandpower shape and every error-bar size you
see today is honest; only the absolute amplitude is hidden. It's additive in Cℓ, so unblinding
is just subtracting the same ΔCℓ.

The hidden cosmology is drawn from the public list on the right — a hundred cosmologies drawn
uniformly around the Planck-18 fiducial in the Ωm–S8 plane (the magnitude is in the bullet and
below), S8 being the lensing amplitude the cross is most sensitive to. You can see the cloud stretch along the S8 degeneracy. The list
itself is public and shareable; the only secret is which entry we picked. That selection is
sealed on the compute node — an OS-entropy integer hashed to an index — so neither I nor the
pipeline ever sees the realized cosmology, and all that's recorded is the commitment hash at the
bottom.

The practical consequence for today: this is a status report read entirely under the blind —
shapes, relative consistency, error-bar sizes — never the amplitude.

On the magnitude: the shift is drawn uniformly within ±0.1 in Ω_m and ±0.075 in S8 — an envelope sized
to cover the S8 tension, so a tension-sized pull can't be reasoned away as "too big to be the blind, so
it must be real." That envelope is public, only the realized draw is secret. The theory we
shift against is computed with pyccl (CCL), our eDR1like pipeline, not an external Boltzmann product.
The likelihood itself, and the move into CLOE, I come back to on the likelihood slide. Bottom line for
this audience: every data vector you see today is blinded.
:::

## Estimators are consistent, GMV a bit low {.data-family}

::: {.fullfig}
![](images/spt26_estimator_robustness.png)

::: {.fullfig-note .nulls-note}
Ongoing validation:<br>spatial splits,<br>$\delta_g/\gamma/\kappa$ nulls,<br>estimator consistency
:::
:::

::: {.notes}
This is a status check on whether the cross depends on which SPT lensing estimator we
feed it. I'm showing one representative high-z bin (bin 5), the two CMB-lensing crosses stacked
top and bottom — cosmic shear × κ and galaxy clustering × κ; the same picture holds across all
six bins. Each panel overlays three SPT-3G estimators — GMV, the SQE pol-only reconstruction
(PP, polarization-only standard quadratic estimator), and the bias + profile-hardened GMV
(GMVbhTTprf) — and the hardened reconstruction sits right on top of GMV; the SQE pol-only
tracks them but with more scatter at high ell.

The message: swapping GMV for the bias + profile-hardened reconstruction — the product
recommended for cross-correlation — moves every bandpower by less than one sigma. Pull RMS
0.29 sigma in both gamma-kappa and delta_g-kappa, all ninety bandpowers inside one sigma, and
the detection S/N doesn't drop — if anything it goes up. The SQE pol-only reconstruction
(PP) is noisier and scatters more at high ell — that's single-channel
reconstruction noise, not a signal or foreground effect — but it stays broadly consistent
within the errors. So the measurement is estimator-robust.

Be careful here, and I want to be honest with this audience because you know lensing
biases cold: this is NOT a foreground-clean certificate. A tSZ or CIB contribution that
is common to GMV and the hardened estimator cancels in the difference — the hardening
correction being small bounds the *part that differs between estimators*, not the total
foreground bias. The direct test is a Websky or Agora-with-HOD recovery, which is
reserved and not yet run. So: estimator-robust, hardening correction bounded below one
sigma — and that's the claim, no more.

The caption points at the wider null-test program this slide is one instance of.
Estimator consistency — what you're looking at — is one member of a family of null
tests we're setting up on all three fields: catalog splits (jackknife halves of the
galaxy samples, which stress the shot-noise model), spatial splits (hemisphere and
patch-level, with the caveat that some spatial splits also split Planck-vs-ground
systematics), and CMB-probe nulls on the κ side — frequency-nulled reconstructions,
the curl mode, half-mission differences. All of them are scored the same way: the
difference of two data vectors against a proper difference covariance —
Cov(ΔC) = C₁₁ + C₂₂ − 2C₁₂ with the cross-block computed through NaMaster — so each
null gets a real χ² and PTE rather than a by-eye call. That machinery exists and is
running today on the settings-validation side; wiring these splits through it is the
program.
:::

## SPT and ACT are consistent, SPT is higher S/N {.data-family}

::: {.fullfig}
![](images/spt26_cross_survey.png)

::: {.fullfig-note .chi2-note}
Naive PTE, considerable<br>footprint overlap
:::
:::

::: {.notes}
This is the cross-survey check. Same Euclid tracers, crossed against two independent
CMB-lensing reconstructions — SPT-3G GMV-hardened in red, ACT DR6 in teal — both laid over the
fiducial theory curve. I'm showing one representative high-z bin (bin 5): shear×κ on top,
clustering×κ on the bottom; the same picture holds across all six bins.

The message is just: we have two κ surveys over this southern overlap, and we can put both
through the identical pipeline on the identical bins. I'm deliberately *not* making an
amplitude or consistency claim here — that arc is blinded and in progress. The transferable
point is that the cross is reproducible across reconstructions, and that gives us a lever:
where SPT constrains better we lean on SPT, where ACT does we lean on ACT.

[SECOND ANGLE — the next slide.] The direct "who constrains where" view: markers placed on
theory, only the error bars real, so the σ(ℓ) of each survey reads off directly — the exact
full Gaussian diagonal for both surveys. ACT is marginally tighter only at the largest scales
(the lowest 2–3 bandpowers, ℓ≲180); **SPT is tighter across the bulk of the range** (ℓ≳200),
by a σ ratio of ~1.5× through the mid-range and up to ~2.5× at ℓ≈2700 — its depth and
resolution win everywhere but the very largest scales.
:::

## SPT-3G tighter for ℓ > 200 {.data-family}

::: {.fullfig}
![](images/spt26_kappa_constraints.png)

::: {.fullfig-note .scale-cuts}
Ongoing validation:<br>$n_{\rm side},$ $\ell_{\rm max},$ apodization,<br>catalog-based $C_\ell$
:::
:::

::: {.notes}
This is the "who constrains where" view — it answers the lever question from the previous
slide. The markers are placed *exactly on the fiducial theory curve* — there's no measured
amplitude here — and each carries its survey's real per-bandpower error bar, σ from the
on-disk covariance. So the whole figure is about the *size* of the error bar, and it's
blinding-safe by construction. Both CMB-lensing crosses: shear×κ on top, clustering×κ on the
bottom — the picture is the same in both.

The story is a crossover around ℓ≈200, and it favors SPT almost everywhere. ACT DR6 is
marginally tighter — by under 10% — only at the very largest scales, the lowest two or three
bandpowers (ℓ ≲ 180), where its wider Euclid overlap gives it more modes. From ℓ≈200 on,
SPT-3G GMV is tighter: its error bar is smaller by a factor of about 1.5 through the mid-range,
growing to about 2.5 by ℓ≈2700, where its depth and angular resolution dominate. The shaded band marks the
SPT-tighter region. So the honest takeaway for this audience: across the bulk of the usable
range SPT is the better-constraining reconstruction on these bins, with ACT competitive only
at the very largest scales.

If asked about the covariance — and this audience will ask: these are the **exact full
data-fiducial Gaussian** per-bandpower σ — the covariance diagonal — for *both* surveys, now
that the full ACT Gaussian exists on disk alongside SPT's. No Knox approximation, no bound: I
slice the bin-5 κ-cross block straight out of each survey's 24-spectrum NaMaster Gaussian
covariance. The crossover sits at ℓ≈200 (γ×κ flips by ℓ≈176, δ_g×κ by ℓ≈221), and it is
*lower* than the Knox-diagonal figure that circulated earlier (ℓ≈250) for a physical reason:
the full Gaussian inflates ACT's low-ℓ variance more than SPT's — ACT's wider Euclid overlap
carries more mode-coupling correction relative to the f_sky-scaled Knox approximation. So the
exact result is, if anything, *more* favorable to SPT than the Knox story. (The ℓ≈1350 number
from much earlier was a different comparison — combined-tomography on the older SACC vector —
not this like-for-like bin-5 one.)

The caption: the scale-cut question is not just "to think about" anymore — validation of the
Cℓ settings is running now. Léa Dumilly has a settings-sweep (script in dr1_cmbx, notebook in
dr1_notebooks) varying nside, ℓ_max, bandpower binning, and the mask apodization scale
against a baseline, with a proper difference covariance — Cov(ΔC) = C₁₁+C₂₂−2C₁₂, the
cross-block computed through NaMaster — so each variant gets a real χ²/PTE, not a by-eye
comparison. Her ℓ_max sweep already shows the kind of effect that will set our cuts: on a
cut sky, bandpowers within a mode-coupling kernel width of the ℓ_max cut bias high, so the
usable range ends *below* wherever we truncate. A comparison of the map-based pseudo-Cℓ
against a catalog-based estimator is planned as part of the same program. That work is on
the tSZ side today but the machinery is the shared pipeline, and running it on these κ
crosses is part of the plan.
:::

## Likelihoods are coming together {.likelihood}

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="54%"}
[In place:]{.colhead} internal `eDR1like`

- **Gaussian likelihood** over any subset of the 6×2pt: NaMaster (or Knox) covariance, Cobaya sampling.
- **Theory**: CCL Limber spectra, HMCode-2020 nonlinear, RSD + magnification (fixed $s(z)$).

---

- **Galaxy bias, fit on RR2 and TR1**: linear $b_i,$ global or per-bin; nonlinear $b_2,$ $b_s$ available.
- **Photo-$z$ marginalization**: per-bin shift $\Delta z_i,$ width-stretch $w_{z,i}.$
:::
::: {.column width="46%"}
[Not yet in the sampled model:]{.colhead}

- **Shear calibration** $m_i,$ **intrinsic alignments** (fixed amplitude, not marginalized).
- **Mock-based covariance**: next slide.

---

[[CLOE](https://euclid-cloe.readthedocs.io):]{.colhead} Euclid's inference framework

- **Theory done, likelihood in progress.**
:::
:::

::: {.notes}
This is the most forward-looking slide, but it's no longer just a plan — the likelihood
machinery is largely in place, so I'll report what's wired and what's still to come. This is
Margherita's eDR1like package, heading toward the v1.0 merge in dr1_cmbx; everything on the
left column I've verified against the code as it stands today.

The architecture, briefly: a Theory layer builds CCL tracers — number counts, weak lensing,
CMB lensing — and computes the angular spectra under Limber; a pure data-vector layer holds
the measured bandpowers, the bandpower windows, and the NaMaster covariance and returns a
Gaussian chi-squared; and a thin adapter exposes it all to Cobaya for sampling. Because
theory and likelihood are separate, Cobaya caches the cosmology while nuisance parameters vary.

What the likelihood can fit: any subset of the full six-by-two-point — all six spectra of
delta-g, gamma, and kappa, selected per run. So yes, the shear auto-spectrum gamma-gamma IS
supported, and kappa-kappa enters here too — this is the "folds in at the likelihood level"
promise from the orientation slide. What we've actually exercised on data so far is narrower
than the capability: the CMB-lensing crosses plus the clustering auto — the gamma-gamma and
kappa-kappa entries are wired but haven't been fit on TR1 yet.

Galaxy bias: fit on both RR2 and TR1 — a linear bias per tomographic bin, either one global
amplitude or per-bin, with second-order and tidal bias terms available in the model.
Magnification bias and RSD are included in the number-counts tracer, but I should be precise:
the magnification slope s(z) is a fixed input — a fitting function or per-bin constants — not
a sampled parameter. Photo-z is marginalized per bin with both a mean shift Δz_i and a
width-stretch w_z,i — the official dndz handling we just merged. Nonlinear power is
HMCode-2020.

On the right, what is NOT yet in the sampled model, and I want to be honest about each.
No multiplicative shear bias m_i exists in the code at all yet. Intrinsic alignments are a
fixed template — a constant-amplitude placeholder in the shear tracer — not a marginalized
nuisance; sampling it is on the list. And the covariance is the analytic NaMaster Gaussian
today; the move to a mock-based covariance — that's what the DEMNUni and FLASK mocks on the
next slide are for — brings with it the finite-mocks corrections: the Hartlap factor, which
debiases the inverse of a noisy covariance estimate, or the Sellentin–Heavens likelihood,
which replaces the Gaussian with a t-distribution that marginalizes over the covariance
uncertainty. Neither is implemented yet because neither is needed until the covariance
actually comes from mocks.

And the bottom line: eDR1like is the working tool today, and we're integrating the CMBX
cross-correlation observable into CLOE, the Euclid consortium inference framework, so it
slots into the official pipeline. The theory side is already done in CLOE; the likelihood
part is in progress. No amplitude numbers on this slide — that arc is blinded and off this
talk; the open amplitude–bias degeneracy question lives on the summary slide.
:::

## Simulations: covariance & systematics

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="48%"}
[Covariance:]{.colhead}

**DEMNUni / FLASK** mocks → mock data vector + mock-based covariance.

[Noise realizations:]{.colhead}

**D1 lensing reconstructions**\
minus truth ($\hat\kappa - \kappa_{\rm true}$) → realistic $\kappa$ noise.

[Cross-covariance [(ambitious)]{.ambitious}:]{.colhead}

**D1 pipeline on Planck FFP10** →\
**Planck / ACT / SPT** cross-covariance.
:::
::: {.column width="52%"}
[Systematics:]{.colhead} three simulated skies

- **Agora:** Euclid-like WL products from its halos + density shells (Marco Gatti, in progress).
- **Flagship:** Euclid side, realistic, one realization — Agora's counterpart.
- **GLASS:** fast lognormal mocks, **known Euclid systematics injected** (extinction, depth, stars…).
  - → could **port the same injections into the Euclid-like Agora mocks**.
:::
:::

::: {.notes}
The simulations leg, in two halves: everything covariance on the left, systematics on the
right.

Covariance. DEMNUni is the CMBX simulation effort — Calabrese, Vielzeuf, Carbone, Fabbian,
Baldi and collaborators, a dedicated mock-simulations paper in prep. It's a purpose-built
end-to-end pipeline: a 2 Gpc/h N-body run across ΛCDM, massive neutrinos at 0.16, 0.32 and
0.53 eV, and f(R) gravity through its sibling DUSTGRAIN; then lightcone, SUBFIND halos,
subhalo-abundance-matched galaxies calibrated to Flagship's galaxy bias and n(z), and
full-sky maps at nside 4096. Because everything comes from the same box, the CMB-lensing
convergence — with ISW–RS — the tomographic WL convergence, and the SHAM galaxy maps are all
correlated; there are even QE lensing reconstructions with Simons Observatory noise. To be
precise about the two jobs: DEMNUni's primary niche is the correlated *signal* mock — the
mock data vector we validate the 6×2pt likelihood against; the covariance proper comes from
the cheap-realization route — FLASK lognormal mocks and Gaussian sims at the DEMNUni
fiducial. That's the same recipe DES×SPT and ACT×DES used: lognormal signal realizations
plus per-experiment reconstruction-noise residuals.

Which is exactly the noise-realizations line: take the D1 mock lensing reconstructions,
subtract the input convergence, and those recon-minus-truth residuals become noise
realizations to add on top of any signal mock — realistic reconstruction noise rather than
an analytic level.

And the ambitious one, which I'll flag as genuinely ambitious: run the D1 lensing pipeline
on the Planck FFP10 lensing simulations, so we can properly estimate the *cross*-covariance
between Planck, ACT, and SPT — the off-diagonal blocks you'd need to combine
reconstructions rather than pick one.

Systematics, on the right — the part I find most interesting. Three simulated skies, each
bringing something different. Agora is the CMB-side sky — extragalactic foregrounds, tSZ,
CIB, radio, all correlated with the same large-scale structure the lensing traces; this
room knows it well. Flagship is the Euclid-side counterpart: the official Euclid galaxy
simulation, gold-standard galaxy realism — though ΛCDM-only, and no CMB lensing. And the
GLASS boxes — let me be clear about what these are, because the name is opaque: fast
lognormal Euclid-like mocks, nothing fancy, whose value is that we inject *known*
systematics — extinction, depth variations, star contamination — and watch what they do to
the cross-spectra. That injection machinery exists in Euclid today.

The plan I want to flag: Marco Gatti is building Euclid-like galaxy and shear products from
the Agora density shells and halo catalogs, and the idea is to port those same systematics
injections into the Agora Euclid mocks — known systematics on top of a realistic correlated
foreground sky. That upgrades the systematics program from one template at a time on the
data — the extinction X_ℓ test we're running on the TR1 catalog — to a controlled
end-to-end test where we know the answer.
:::

::: {.notes}
Quick wrap. Where we are, three honest lines. First: the Euclid data products are still evolving — we're on TR1 cycle 1, and the sequence runs cycle 1 to cycle 2 to DR1, each pass firmer than the last. Second: both CMB-lensing cross data vectors are measured — density–kappa and shear–kappa — under a provisional self-blind, one we'll retire for the collaboration blinding later. Third, and I want to be honest here: the estimator and cross-survey agreement you've seen is qualitative — the curves sit on top of each other — but we have not yet quantified it rigorously, and doing that properly needs a real covariance, which is the mock (cross)-covariance line on the right. That's the status: infrastructure in place, agreement by eye, rigour still to come.

Then the two columns of work in flight — and I mean genuinely in flight, this is what we're doing right now. Systematics and null tests, three families: null tests — random-position/shot-noise maps, spatial and magnitude/colour splits, and the κ B-mode and curl nulls; consistency — the cross holds across CMB reconstructions (SPT, ACT, Planck) and across Euclid shear pipelines (LensMC versus METACAL); and the map-systematics budget — each contamination template (depth, stellar density, extinction, PSF, zodiacal, exposures…) is NaMaster-deprojected and χ²-tested for whether it moves the spectrum, with extinction the one we've already pushed end-to-end on TR1. On the bias and modeling side: galaxy bias and magnification bias are fit on both RR2 and TR1; the shear multiplicative bias m_i, intrinsic-alignment marginalization, and n(z) marginalization (the photo-z shift and width nuisances) are the next nuisances into the sampled model; and the measurement-definition checks — where to cut in ℓ, the apodization scale, and the move from analytic to mock-based covariance — are running as part of the same program.

And the headline of the next line: we're planning to run our first chain soon — the joint likelihood, sampled under the blind. Everything on this slide funnels into that: the likelihood machinery from the likelihood slide is in place, the data vector is sealed, and the systematics and modeling checks are what stand between us and trusting the posterior.

And the last beat: this is TR1 cycle 1, the first pass of the timeline from the opening slide. Ahead is TR cycle 2 and eventually DR1, and the point of the iteration structure is exactly that the processing improves and stabilizes each time — catalogs, masks, calibration all firm up, and the analysis choices we're validating now carry forward onto better data. So the status today is the foundation pass, not the final word.

Deliberately no amplitude number on this slide — that arc is blinded and in progress, so I'm reporting status, not a result.

Thanks to the Euclid CMBX SWG — Margherita Lembo, Louis Legrand, Giulio Fabbian and the 3×2pt+κ team — and to the SPT-3G lensing team, whose winter GMV kappa maps make this whole cross possible. Happy to take questions.
:::
